questions.q: In the real end-to-end flow, what typically happens first when something breaks?
options: Incident management logs, categorizes, prioritizes, and resolves it, often with a workaround
Change enablement immediately authorizes a fix before anything is logged
Problem management opens a known error before the incident is even logged
The service desk waits for a pattern to emerge before doing anything
questions.explain: The loop starts with incident management restoring service, which may happen with no root cause known yet.

questions.q: What typically triggers problem management to get involved after an incident is resolved?
options: The same failure recurs, or its cause isn't understood even though the symptom was fixed
Every single incident automatically becomes a problem record
Problem management only gets involved after a change fails
An incident can never lead to a problem investigation
questions.explain: Most incidents end at resolution; the loop continues into problem management only when recurrence or unresolved cause makes that necessary.

questions.q: Why can't problem management simply implement its own fix once root cause is identified?
options: Because altering a configuration item is a change, which must go through change enablement's risk assessment and authorization
Because problem management is not allowed to identify root causes
Because known errors are always resolved without touching production
Because incident management must approve every problem record first
questions.explain: Diagnosing a cause doesn't carry authority to change production; that step belongs to change enablement regardless of which practice found the cause.

questions.q: A known error's fix is actively needed right now to stop a major incident. Which path does ITIL 4 suggest for implementing that fix?
options: An emergency change, authorized quickly but still through a real, expedited authorization process
No change is needed since the cause is already documented as a known error
A standard change, since the fix has already been performed before
The fix should bypass change enablement entirely given the urgency
questions.explain: Urgency from an active major incident is exactly the scenario ITIL 4 describes for emergency changes — fast, but still authorized.

questions.q: What is the business value of running incident, problem, and change as a connected loop rather than three separate silos?
options: The business keeps running during the disruption, the real cause doesn't stay a mystery, and the eventual fix goes in without causing a new incident
It eliminates the need for authorization on any future changes
It means incidents no longer need to be logged individually
It allows problem management to skip root cause analysis entirely
questions.explain: Each practice closes a different gap: restoration, root cause, and safe implementation — together closing the loop back to fewer future incidents.
